new_statements.quote: As it is stated in the works of Azeb (1996: 114), in Wolaitta, each lexical item in its simple/citation form receives only one high tonal accent though the assignment of the tonal accent is unpredictable. This is true in Gofa, too, for the simple nouns, adjectives, and adverbs in their citation forms receive only one high tonal accent either on the terminal vowels or on the penultimate vowels. [...] Gofa too, is a tonal accent language [...] The high tonal accent is assigned on the second mora of the accented long syllable in Gofa [...] Based on this fact, we can claim that Gofa is not a stress language since the domain of a stress is the syllable as a whole.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Gofa (one of the three languages formerly lumped under [gmo]) has no stress; it is a tonal-accent language: every simple noun, adjective or adverb in citation form carries exactly one high tonal accent, on either the final vowel or the penultimate vowel, and which of the two is lexically unpredictable; in an accented long syllable the H sits on the second mora. Verbs assign the H according to their affixes. Sibling languages: Gamo — Hayward 1994 / Hayward & Chabo 2014 analyse it as tonal accent with one H per tone phrase (on the last root syllable of an 'accentuated' word, else by default on the terminal vowel; H only on the first word of the phrase), while Thomassen 2015 (Bonke Gamo) rejects the accent analysis in favour of plain H/L tone; Dawro — Tariku Negese 2010 classifies it as a register tone language with H and L, lexical and grammatical, with no stress statement (Allan 1976 had called pitch 'predictable and non-contrastive').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by any source; Sellassie Cheru 2015 says compound nouns and phrases may carry one or multiple tonal accents (sec. 5.2.2).
new_statements.exceptions: Placement of the single H (final vs penultimate) is lexically unpredictable in Gofa; verbs differ by affixation; Hayward & Chabo 2014 (per Thomassen 2015: 115) posit many exceptional tone patterns in Gamo, notably negative verb paradigms.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms of simple words; in Gofa and Gamo the accent/H is a phrase-level property (one H per tone phrase, on the first word) — Hayward 1994: 487 as quoted by Thomassen 2015: 87; Sellassie Cheru 2015 sec. 4.3.2 pp. 86-88 on H-spreading and sentence-type H on the finite verb. Whether the term 'stress' even applies is denied explicitly for Gofa and implicitly (tone-language analyses) for Gamo and Dawro.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: gamo1244 is not a language. It is Glottolog's bookkeeping node for ISO 639-3 [gmo] "Gamo-Gofa-Dawro", which ISO change request 2008-080 (SIL Ethiopia, adopted 2009-01-16; saved as, p. 3 rationale: separate ethnolinguistic identities and language-development projects, lexical similarity among the three no greater than with Wolaytta per Girard 2002) split into Gamo [gmv] = gamo1243, Gofa [gof] = gofa1235 and Dawro [dwr] = dawr1236. Glottolog attaches zero descriptive references to gamo1244. by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) (a retired code does not make a separate language; counts are distinct entities, not records) the catalog should carry no gamo1244 row; the stress/accent statements belong to the three successor entries: gofa1235 (Sellassie Cheru 2015: tonal-accent language, H on final or penultimate vowel, unpredictable; 'not a stress language'), gamo1243 (Thomassen 2015: tone language, H+L, no accent; vs Hayward 1994 / Hayward & Chabo 2014: tonal accent, one H per tone phrase on the accented last root syllable or by default the terminal vowel), dawr1236 (Tariku Negese 2010: register tone language, H/L, lexical and grammatical; no stress statement). The Dawro files downloaded here (Tariku 2010, Alebachew 2010, Hanserud 2018) are new to our check and should be copied to dawr1236/, whose earlier scan classification was the named source could not be reached for exactly Tariku 2010.

sources.citation: Hanserud, Sigurd. 2018. Dawro verb morphology and syntax: A description. MA thesis, University of Oslo. xi+136 pp. (Glottolog ref 620718)
sources.note: Sec. 2.1.1 Pitch, p. 15 (PDF 27): 'Allan (1976) writes that pitch normally is non-contrastive, but with some exceptions'; contrastive-pitch pairs from Allan/Alebachew; 'Hirut (2007), on the other hand, does not mention pitch'; the tone-vs-pitch accent question is left open ('tone has not proven an obstacle during elicitation'). No stress statement.

sources.citation: Thomassen, Aïda Leistad. 2015. namʔú masará gawarata. Contributions to the description of the phonology of the Bonke variety of Gamo. MA thesis, University of Oslo. 180 pp. (Glottolog ref 577907, Gamo gamo1243)
sources.note: Ch. 6 Tonology. p. 87 (PDF 104) block-quotes Hayward 1994:487: 'That it is accentual is evidenced by the fact that prosodic prominence - in this case, the higher pitch feature - has a culminative function; it must occur in every word uttered in isolation, but never more than once; it must appear in each phrase, but only on the first word.' p. 88 (PDF 105) quotes Hayward & Chabo 2014:55: 'Gamo is best described as a tonal-accent language'. sources.citation: Alebachew Biadgie. 2010. Verb Complements in Dawro: A Descriptive Approach. MA thesis, Addis Ababa University. 72 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 1.9.2 Tone, pp. 10-12 (PDF 18-20): reviews Allan 1976:328 (Dawro a 'pitch language' with two levels of systematic pitch; pairs bàná 'I will go' / báná 'dust'), Hiwot 1988:22 and Hirut 2007:99 (imperative/jussive final syllable with high pitch), Siseraw 1989 (tone language, H and L); own pairs yédd 'send' / yèdd 'resign'; 'it is possible to consider Dawro as a tone language. However, the tone of the language needs further investigation.' No stress statement.

sources.citation: Tariku Negese. 2010. Aspects of Dauro Phonology. MA thesis, Department of Linguistics, Addis Ababa University. 79 pp. (Glottolog ref 589720, Dawro dawr1236)
sources.note: Sec. 3.4 Tone, pp. 58-61 (PDF 69-72): 'this work substantiates that tone is contrastive and is not perfectly predictable. Therefore, this work accordingly categorizes Dauro as a tone language particularly a register tone language which uses two level tones; high and low that are realized as raising and falling pitch across words.' Minimal pairs k'eesaa 'priest' / k'éesáa 'colostrum', mek'etsaa 'bone' / mék'étsáa 'clan'; tone has lexical and (probably) grammatical function. Reviews Allan 1976:332 ('pitch is predictable and non-contrastive') vs Siseraw 1989 (two level tones, most words end L).…
